The authors questioned whether the inclusion of children aged 12–14 years might exceed the age range where household conditions influence health outcomes. 2. Breysse et al. (2015) conducted a quasi-experimental study to evaluate self-reported health outcomes, including mental health, physical health, and falls, before and after implementing a green renovation package in public housing for elderly residents. The renovations included new insulation, exterior cladding, air sealing, and window replacement. 3. Bray et al. (2017) performed a cohort study assessing the costs and outcomes of population health improvements through social housing upgrades, such as installing new boilers and double-glazing. The study found no significant effect on the main tenant's quality of life. 4. Grey et al. (2017) conducted a quasi-experimental study to assess the short-term health and psychosocial impacts of energy efficiency upgrades in low-income households. The intervention included external wall insulation and heating upgrades. While there were no significant improvements in mental health, physical health, respiratory symptoms, or asthma symptoms, the study highlighted the need for further investigation. 5. Homøe et al. (1999) examined the relationship between socioeconomic risk factors and acute otitis media (AOM) in Greenlandic children aged 3–5 and 8 years. No association was found between insulation standards and episodes of AOM. 6. Howden-Chapman et al. (2007) conducted a cluster randomized controlled trial (RCT) to evaluate the effects of insulating existing homes on health inequalities in low-income households. The intervention included draft-stopping and the installation of ceiling and under-floor insulation. The study reported reductions in self-reported wheezing, fewer days off school or work, and fewer general practitioner (GP) visits, but no significant changes in hospital admissions. 7. Iversen et al. (1986) used a questionnaire to assess changes in respiratory symptoms, such as eye irritation and dry throat, among tenants after window replacements for improved air-tightness. Although odds ratios for these symptoms were lower, they did not reach statistical significance. The study had a high risk of selection bias. 8. Poortinga et al. (2017) conducted a repeated cross-sectional survey over five waves to evaluate the social and health outcomes of upgrades to national housing standards in Wales. Improvements in mental health and respiratory health were associated with new windows, doors, loft insulation, and external wall insulation. However, cavity wall insulation was linked to worsened mental health, respiratory symptoms, and general health. 9. Preval et al. (2017) conducted a quasi-experimental retrospective cohort study to assess the impact of improved insulation and heating on mortality risk in adults aged 65+ with prior cardiovascular or respiratory hospitalizations. Mortality rates were lower in the insulated group for those with circulatory illnesses but showed no significant difference for respiratory illnesses. Potential bias remained due to the possibility that insulation installation reflected better health or socioeconomic conditions. 10. Tavernier et al. The study found no difference in asthma rates between children with different glazing systems, as assessed by a questionnaire. 11. Telfar Barnard et al. (2011) evaluated the effects of retrofitted insulation and new heaters on health service utilization, pharmaceutical costs, and mortality in New Zealand. The study found no significant effect on hospitalizations or pharmaceutical prescriptions but reported lower mortality rates in adults aged 65+ previously hospitalized for circulatory illnesses. Despite matching, potential bias remained due to the possibility that insulation installation reflected better health or socioeconomic circumstances.
